text.p: Here are highlights of stories reported by Hungary's press, based on information by Nepszabadsag's Hungary Around the Clock service. For further details on how to subscribe to Hungary Around the Clock, please contact Monica Kovacs at (361) 351 7142 or fax your request to (361) 351 7141.

- Today Parliament is expected to vote against the renomination of Janos Bruhacs to one of the three vacant Constitutional Court posts. Yesterday Parliament began general debate on financial support for local governments in 1997.

- The Supreme Court yesterday affirmed an earlier Capital's Court ruling that the election of Christian Democratic Party executives last December was invalid. The election, at which party president Gyorgy Giczy was re-elected, was unlawfully convened by Giczy against party rules.
- Former Free Democrat president Ivan Peto will be a member of Parliament's budget committee.

- A police document shows that information was collected on lawyer Marta Tocsik last year via secret service methods. Peter Liszkai, a former senior legal counsel with the State Privatisation and Holding Co., said he found two bugging devices in Tocsik's flat.

- Czech Industry and Trade Minister Vladimir Dlouhy said in Budapest that Prague will consider a Hungarian request to ease import deposit measures introduced last Monday, but he ruled out sweeping changes.
- Finance Ministry political state secretary Laszlo Akar and World Bank vice-poresident Johannes Linn signed a $225 million structural adjustment loan at the Bank's Washington headquarters on Monday.
- Kreditanstalt fur Wiederaufbau is interested in financing construction of the new metro line in Budapest, board chairman Gert Vogt said after meeting Minister Karoly Lotz on Monday.
- A report on Postabank's 1996 figures shows after-tax profits of 5.6 million forints as opposed to 3.165 billion in the preliminary report sent to the stock exchange in February.

- A faction with the Socialist Party known as the Social Democratic Group would dismiss Prime Minister Gyula Horn from the post of party president, although it considers his merits to be beyond any doubt, according to a copy of a draft.

- Hungary has passed the most painful phase of economic austerity, but 1998 will not be an easy ride either, National Bank president Gyorgy Suranyi told the Vienna daily Die Presse, as reported in Hungarian dailies.
